verifications.claim_text: cognitive load during revision was significantly lower after direct corrections on grammatical errors than after metalinguistic codes on grammatical and non-grammatical errors
verifications.evidence_quote: Based on self-reporting, the cognitive load imposed by revision after DCF+G was significantly lower than that after ME+GN (p < 0.001, SE = 0.350).
verifications.explanation: The central assertion — that self-reported cognitive load after revision with direct corrections on grammatical errors (DCF+G) was significantly lower than after metalinguistic codes on grammatical and non-grammatical errors (ME+GN) — is stated directly in section 5.4: "the cognitive load imposed by revision after DCF+G was significantly lower than that after ME+GN (p < 0.001, SE = 0.350)", and corroborated in Table 3 ("***ME+GN > DCF+G 1.91 [0.95, 2.88]") and the conclusion ("learners’ cognitive load estimates proved significantly lower when corrections were provided directly and they targeted grammatical issues only"). The peripheral assertions (cognitive load measured via self-report/mental-effort scale after text revision; the two named feedback conditions) are also supported by the methods and results sections. No contradiction and no hedge removal.

verifications.claim_text: the majority of 33 students actively engaged with combined automated, peer, and teacher feedback, and the approach promoted behavioural, affective, and cognitive engagement and encouraged thoughtful revisions
verifications.evidence_quote: We found that the majority of students actively engaged with this integrated approach and that it effectively promoted students’ behavioural, affective, and cognitive engagement with feedback on their writing and encouraged thoughtful revisions.
verifications.explanation: The abstract states the claim almost verbatim: "We found that the majority of students actively engaged with this integrated approach and that it effectively promoted students' behavioural, affective, and cognitive engagement with feedback on their writing and encouraged thoughtful revisions." The 33-student sample is confirmed in the abstract ("a group of 33 students") and Methods ("one teacher and 33 students at a Chinese university"), and the integrated approach is defined as combining "automated, peer, and teacher feedback." The body corroborates the engagement findings (88% submitted to AWE more than five times; 91% positive attitudes; all seven revision operation types used). The paper does note that some students failed to engage, but this is consistent with "the majority" rather than contradicting it.
